questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the path of magnetic field lines around and through a bar magnet?
options: They form continuous closed loops, running from north to south outside a magnet
They begin on north poles and end on south poles, both inside and outside a magnet
They form continuous closed loops, running from south to north outside a magnet
They begin on south poles and end on north poles, both inside and outside a magnet
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end: they run from north to south outside a magnet and continue from south to north inside it, forming closed loops. This is a key difference from electric field lines, which start and end on charges.

questions.stem: On a magnetic field diagram, how is the strength of the field shown?
options: By how sharply the field lines curve
By how close together the field lines are
By how long each field line is drawn
By the size of the arrowheads on the lines
questions.explanation: The field is strongest where the lines are closest together, such as near the poles of a bar magnet. The arrows show the field's direction, not its strength.

questions.stem: What is the unit of magnetic field strength?
options: Weber (Wb)
Newton per coulomb (N C⁻¹)
Henry (H)
Tesla (T)
questions.explanation: Magnetic field strength, B, is measured in tesla. The newton per coulomb is the unit of electric field strength, and the weber is the unit of magnetic flux.

questions.stem: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point found from a field line diagram?
options: It is along a straight line from that point towards the nearest north pole
It is along a straight line from the nearest south pole towards that point
It is along the tangent to the field line at that point, in the direction of the arrow
It is perpendicular to the field line at that point, pointing away from the magnet
questions.explanation: The field direction at any point is the tangent to the field line there, following its arrow. It is the direction the north pole of a small compass would point. Field lines curve, so the direction is not simply towards a pole.

questions.stem: A small compass is placed near the north pole of a bar magnet, on the magnet's axis. Which way does the compass needle's north end point?
options: Away from the magnet, along the field line
Towards the magnet's north pole
At right angles to the magnet's axis
Towards the Earth's geographic north
questions.explanation: Field lines leave the north pole, so near it on the axis the field points away from the magnet. A compass needle's north end lines up with the field, so it points away; like poles repel. Close to a strong magnet, the magnet's field dominates the Earth's.

questions.stem: Why can magnetic field lines never cross?
options: Crossing lines would need a north pole at the crossing point, which cannot exist
The field is the same strength everywhere, so the lines must be kept parallel
The field has only one direction at each point, and crossing lines would show two
The field lines repel each other, because they carry like magnetic charges
questions.explanation: A field line shows the direction of the field at each point. If two lines crossed, there would be two directions at one place, which is impossible: the combined field has a single direction there. Field lines are a model, not physical objects that repel each other.

questions.stem: Two bar magnets are placed end to end with their north poles facing each other a short distance apart. Which describes the field between them?
options: The lines run straight from one north pole to the other, with the strongest field midway
The lines form closed loops between the two poles, with a uniform field midway
The lines run from each north pole into the other magnet, through its north pole
The lines from each pole bend away sideways, with a neutral point of zero field midway
questions.explanation: Like poles repel, so the field lines from the two north poles push away from each other and curve out sideways. Midway, the two fields are equal and opposite, giving a neutral point where the field is zero. Lines running straight across would describe a north pole facing a south pole.

questions.stem: Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet show the shape of its field. What extra information does a small plotting compass give?
options: The direction of the field at each point
The strength of the field in tesla
The temperature of the magnet
The material the magnet is made of
questions.explanation: Iron filings line up along the field lines, showing their shape, but a filing has no marked north end, so it cannot show which way the field points. A compass needle's north end points along the field, giving its direction.

questions.stem: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long, straight wire carrying a current?
options: Straight lines pointing radially outward from the wire in all directions
Concentric circles around the wire, evenly spaced at all distances
Concentric circles around the wire, spaced further apart with distance
Straight lines running parallel to the wire, in the direction of the current
questions.explanation: The field lines are circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it. The field weakens with distance, so the circles are drawn further apart further from the wire. Radial lines describe the electric field of a charged wire.

questions.stem: A long straight wire carries a current directly out of the page. Viewed from the front, what is the direction of the magnetic field around it?
options: Straight lines to the right
Anticlockwise circles
Clockwise circles
Radially outward lines
questions.explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, point the right thumb along the current (out of the page) and the fingers curl in the direction of the field: anticlockwise. A current into the page gives clockwise circles.

questions.stem: What is the magnetic field strength 5.0 cm from a long straight wire carrying 10 A? Use μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
questions.explanation: B = μ₀I/2πr = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 0.050) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Leaving the distance as 5.0 instead of 0.050 m gives 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ T, a hundred times too small.

questions.stem: The magnetic field 2.0 cm from a long straight wire is B. What is it 4.0 cm from the wire, with the same current?
options: 2B
B
questions.explanation: For a long straight wire, B = μ₀I/2πr, so B is inversely proportional to r, not to r². Doubling the distance halves the field. A quarter would follow from the inverse square law, which applies to a point charge's electric field.

questions.stem: The magnetic field 10 cm from a long straight wire is 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Using μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, what current does the wire carry?
questions.explanation: Rearranging B = μ₀I/2πr gives I = 2πrB/μ₀ = (2π × 0.10 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(4π × 10⁻⁷) = 10 A. Using r = 0.010 m gives 1.0 A and r = 1.0 m gives 100 A; the distance must be 0.10 m.

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires 20 cm apart each carry 5.0 A, in opposite directions. Using μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, what is the magnetic field midway between them?
options: 0 T
questions.explanation: Each wire alone gives B = μ₀I/2πr = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 5.0)/(2π × 0.10) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ T at the midpoint. With opposite currents, the right-hand grip rule shows both fields point the same way between the wires, so they add to 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Currents in the same direction would cancel there.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire runs north-south directly above a compass. When a current flows north along the wire, which way does the compass needle's north end swing?
options: It stays pointing north
Towards the west
Towards the east
Upward, towards the wire
questions.explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, with the thumb pointing north along the current, the field lines curl so that below the wire the field points west. The compass needle swings towards that field. This is the effect Oersted observed, showing that currents produce magnetic fields.

questions.stem: Wire P carries 4.0 A and wire Q carries 2.0 A. How does the magnetic field 1.0 cm from P compare with the field 2.0 cm from Q?
options: It is eight times as large
It is four times as large
It is twice as large
It is the same
questions.explanation: B = μ₀I/2πr, so B is proportional to I/r. For P, I/r = 4.0/1.0 = 4.0; for Q, I/r = 2.0/2.0 = 1.0. The field near P is four times as large. Treating the field as falling with 1/r² would give eight times.

questions.stem: What does the magnetic field of a single circular loop of wire carrying a current look like?
options: Lines are straight and parallel to the plane of the loop, both inside and outside
Lines pass through the centre at right angles to the loop, like a short bar magnet
Lines form circles in the plane of the loop, concentric with the loop and outside it
Lines run radially outward from the centre of the loop in the plane of the loop
questions.explanation: Each section of wire produces circular field lines around itself. Inside the loop these all point the same way, so the field at the centre is strong and perpendicular to the loop's plane. The overall pattern resembles that of a short bar magnet, with a north face and a south face.

questions.stem: A circular loop lies in the plane of the page, and its current flows anticlockwise as you look at it. What is the direction of the magnetic field at its centre?
options: Into the page, away from you, so the face you see acts as a north pole
Out of the page, towards you, so the face you see acts as a south pole
In the plane of the page, pointing towards the top of the loop
Out of the page, towards you, so the face you see acts as a north pole
questions.explanation: Applying the right-hand grip rule to any part of the loop shows the field inside pointing out of the page. Field lines leave a north pole, so the face towards you acts as a north pole. A clockwise current would make that face a south pole.

questions.stem: What is a solenoid?
options: A long helical coil of insulated wire that makes a magnetic field when current flows
A single straight wire carrying a large current, which produces circular magnetic field lines
A permanent bar magnet made from soft iron, which keeps its magnetic field without current
A flat circular loop of bare wire, which produces a magnetic field only at its centre
questions.explanation: A solenoid is many turns of insulated wire wound into a long coil. The fields of all the turns combine to give a strong, uniform field inside the coil when a current flows. Adding an iron core turns it into an electromagnet.

questions.stem: Which describes the magnetic field of a current-carrying solenoid?
options: Like a bar magnet outside, with the field weakest at the centre inside
Like a bar magnet outside, with strong, uniform, parallel field lines inside
Concentric circles around the coil, with no field at all inside it
Radial lines spreading from the middle of the coil in every direction
questions.explanation: The fields of the turns reinforce inside the coil, giving closely spaced, parallel lines: a strong, uniform field. Outside, the pattern looks like a bar magnet's, with the lines looping from one end to the other.

questions.stem: How can the right-hand grip rule be used to find the north pole of a solenoid?
options: Curl the fingers in the direction of the conventional current in the turns; the thumb points to the south end
Curl the fingers in the direction of the conventional current in the turns; the thumb points to the north end
Point the thumb in the direction of the conventional current in the turns; the fingers curl towards the north end
Curl the fingers in the direction of the electron flow in the turns; the thumb points to the north end
questions.explanation: For a solenoid, the right-hand fingers curl around the coil in the direction of conventional current, and the thumb points along the field inside, towards the north end. Using electron flow would give the opposite end.

questions.stem: What happens to the poles of a solenoid when the direction of the current is reversed?
options: Both ends become north poles
The field disappears completely
The north and south poles swap ends
The poles stay where they are
questions.explanation: The field direction follows the current direction, so reversing the current reverses the field and swaps the poles. The field strength is unchanged if the size of the current is unchanged.

questions.stem: A solenoid 0.25 m long has 500 turns and carries 2.0 A. Using μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, what is the magnetic field strength inside it?
questions.explanation: B = μ₀NI/L = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 500 × 2.0/0.25 ≈ 5.0 × 10⁻³ T. Forgetting to divide by the length gives 1.3 × 10⁻³ T, and multiplying by L instead of dividing gives 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ T.

questions.stem: A solenoid is compressed to half its length, keeping the same number of turns and the same current. What happens to the field inside it?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It quadruples
questions.explanation: B = μ₀NI/L, so with N and I unchanged, halving L doubles B. The turns are packed twice as closely, so twice as many turns per metre contribute to the field.

questions.stem: A new solenoid has twice as many turns and is twice as long as an old one, and carries the same current. How does the field inside compare?
options: It is twice as large
It is four times as large
It is half as large
It is the same
questions.explanation: The field depends on the number of turns per unit length, N/L, and the current. Doubling both N and L leaves N/L unchanged, so B = μ₀NI/L is the same.

questions.stem: Solenoid A has 200 turns over 0.10 m and carries 1.0 A. Solenoid B has 400 turns over 0.40 m and carries 1.5 A. What is the ratio of the field in A to the field in B?
questions.explanation: A has 2000 turns per metre, so B_A ∝ 2000 × 1.0 = 2000. B has 1000 turns per metre, so B_B ∝ 1000 × 1.5 = 1500. The ratio is 2000/1500 ≈ 1.3. Ignoring the lengths gives (200 × 1.0)/(400 × 1.5) ≈ 0.33, and inverting the correct ratio gives 0.75.

questions.stem: What current is needed in a long solenoid with 2000 turns per metre to produce a field of 0.010 T inside it? Use μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Rearranging B = μ₀(N/L)I gives I = B/(μ₀N/L) = 0.010/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000) ≈ 4.0 A. Dividing μ₀(N/L) by B instead gives 0.25, and slips with powers of ten give 0.40 A or 40 A.

questions.stem: A long solenoid is replaced by one with twice the diameter but the same length, number of turns and current. What happens to the field strength inside?
options: It falls to a quarter
It stays the same
It halves
It doubles
questions.explanation: For a long solenoid, B = μ₀NI/L depends only on the turns per unit length and the current; the diameter does not appear. The wider solenoid has a field of the same strength spread over a larger cross-section.

questions.stem: Why is soft iron used as the core of an electromagnet such as a scrapyard lifting magnet?
options: It keeps its magnetism after the current stops, so the magnet keeps working without power
It conducts electricity better than copper, so a larger current flows through the coil
It is not attracted by magnets, so it does not interfere with the solenoid's own field
It is easily magnetised when current flows and loses its magnetism when current stops
questions.explanation: Soft iron's domains align readily with the solenoid's field, greatly strengthening it, and return to random orientations when the current is switched off. That lets a scrapyard magnet pick up and then release its load. A core that kept its magnetism could not drop the load.

questions.stem: Steel keeps much of its magnetism after the magnetising field is removed. What does this make it suitable for?
options: Permanent magnets, but not the cores of electromagnets that need to switch off
The cores of electromagnets that need to be switched on and off quickly
Connecting wires, because magnetised steel conducts current more easily
Neither use, because a material that keeps its magnetism cannot be magnetised
questions.explanation: A material that retains its magnetism, such as steel, is magnetically hard and makes a good permanent magnet. An electromagnet that must release its load or reverse its field needs a soft magnetic material, such as soft iron, that demagnetises easily.

questions.stem: Why does inserting an iron core into a current-carrying solenoid make the field much stronger?
options: The solenoid's field aligns the iron's magnetic domains, and their fields add to it
The iron conducts the current more easily, so the current in the solenoid increases
The iron increases the number of turns per metre in the solenoid's coil of wire
The iron stores electric charge, which produces an extra magnetic field of its own
questions.explanation: Iron is ferromagnetic: it is made of tiny regions called domains, each a small magnet. The solenoid's field lines them up, so their fields add to the solenoid's field, making it many times stronger. The core is insulated from the coil, so it carries no current.

questions.stem: A student replaces the iron core of an electromagnet with a copper rod of the same size. What happens to the strength of the electromagnet?
options: It falls to about that of the coil alone, because copper is not ferromagnetic
It rises, because copper is a better conductor of electricity than iron
It stays the same, because the core material plays no part in the field
It rises, because copper's domains align more easily than iron's do
questions.explanation: Copper is not ferromagnetic, so it has no domains to align and adds almost nothing to the field; the electromagnet is about as strong as an air-cored coil. The core's electrical conductivity is not what matters.

questions.stem: Which set of changes would all make an electromagnet stronger?
options: More current, more turns of wire, and an aluminium core
More current, more turns of wire, and a soft iron core
Less current, more turns of wire, and a copper core
More current, fewer turns of wire, and a soft iron core
questions.explanation: The field of a solenoid grows with the current and the number of turns per unit length, and a soft iron core multiplies it further. Copper and aluminium are not ferromagnetic, so they do not strengthen the field.

questions.stem: Why is an electromagnet, rather than a permanent magnet, used in an electric door lock that must release when a switch is pressed?
options: Its field points in every direction at once, so it holds the door from any side
Its field depends on the current, so it can be switched on and off or varied
Its field is always stronger than that of any permanent magnet of the same size
Its field does not need a power supply, so it keeps working in a blackout
questions.explanation: An electromagnet produces a field only while current flows, and its strength can be changed by changing the current. Cutting the current releases the lock. A permanent magnet's field cannot be switched off, and an electromagnet does need a power supply.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the number of turns on an electromagnet affects how many paperclips it can lift. Which variables must be kept constant?
options: Only the current, because nothing else affects an electromagnet
The current, the core, the length of the coil and the type of paperclip
The number of turns, the current and the type of paperclip used
The number of paperclips lifted, the current and the core material
questions.explanation: The number of turns is the independent variable and the number of paperclips lifted is the dependent variable. Everything else that affects the strength, such as the current, the core, the coil length and the paperclips used to measure it, must be controlled for a valid test.

questions.stem: An electromagnet lifts 8 paperclips at 1.0 A and 16 at 2.0 A, but only 18 at 4.0 A. What best explains the result at 4.0 A?
options: The current has stopped producing a magnetic field above 2.0 A in the solenoid
The paperclips have become magnetised and now repel each other more and more
The iron core has become permanently magnetised and no longer responds to current
The iron core is approaching saturation, with most of its domains already aligned
questions.explanation: At first the field, and so the number of paperclips, rises in proportion to the current. Once most of the iron's domains are aligned, the core cannot add much more field, so further increases in current give only small gains. The coil's own field still rises with current.
